title: Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries
desc: The risk of developing dementia at any given age has fallen steadily in Europe and the United States over recent decades. A key unresolved question is whether recent generations reach older age with better cognitive capacity, experience slower cognitive decline, or both, as this has implications for when preventive interventions are likely to have the greatest impact. Analyzing ~783,000 episodic-memory assessments from ~219,000 individuals in five longitudinal studies followed for up to 30 years, we find that later-born generations benefit from a double dividend, with higher memory levels entering old age and slower decline thereafter. The combined advantage is large enough to plausibly account for the reported 13% per-decade decline in dementia incidence. Improvements are concentrated among the fastest decliners; later-born generations show longer periods of stable memory, and their slower decline is mirrored by lower rates of clinical impairment and slower hippocampal atrophy. Calendar-time trends affecting all generations simultaneously are unlikely to explain these differences. Because memory level is built mainly in early life whereas the rate of decline is shaped by conditions in adulthood, sustaining the decline in dementia incidence will require prevention policies that protect brain health across the whole lifespan, beginning in childhood.

title: FIRE-EVIDENCE: enabling LLM-driven, machine-readable evidence synthesis for women’s health
desc: Clinical evidence is abundant in the published literature yet remains fragmented and underutilized, particularly in women’s health and menopause, where timely, personalized decision-making is critical. Conventional evidence synthesis relies on resource-intensive manual review, limiting scalability and delaying translation into practice, while automated approaches often produce outputs that are not directly computable or integrable into decision-support workflows. We present FIRE-EVIDENCE, a large language model framework that transforms full-text clinical studies into structured, Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR)-aligned computable evidence. The pipeline was optimized on seven development documents and evaluated on two datasets: a primary dataset of 26 expert-annotated randomized controlled trials and a secondary dataset of 18 studies derived from five systematic reviews. Across expert-annotated trials, FIRE-EVIDENCE achieved 94.35% completeness, 94.61% correctness, 97.36% source faithfulness, and an F1 score of 94.43%. FHIR-compliance testing in a 10-output native FHIR-R5 subset showed that all validated outputs passed base HL7 FHIR validation without errors. FIRE-EVIDENCE demonstrates a feasible pathway for standard-based, machine-readable evidence synthesis.

title: Beyond scales: Artificial intelligence, language, and behavior in suicide risk modeling-a narrative review.
source: PubMed · European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology
desc: [European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology] Suicide is a leading, preventable cause of premature mortality, yet identifying individuals at imminent risk remains difficult. There are no validated biomarkers for routine stratification, and common approaches (clinical interviews, rating scales, self-report) are limited by subjectivity, reporting bias, and weak positive predictive value for rare outcomes. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI)-including machine learning, deep learning, and large language models-offer opportunities to integrate heterogeneous signals relevant to risk and treatment response. This narrative review summarizes recent AI-enabled prediction and characterization of suicidal thoughts and behaviors across major data modalities: structured electronic health records and claims; natural language processing of clinical notes and digital text; speech and facial/behavioral signals; neuroimaging and other neurobiological measures; and passive sensing from smartphones and wearables. We review common modeling and evaluation practices, emphasizing clinically relevant performance assessment (discrimination and calibration) and the importance of temporal and external validation. We also highlight barriers to translation, including class imbalance and label noise, dataset shift across sites and time, limited prospective evaluation, and the need for interpretable outputs that can support medication decisions and care pathways (e.g., triage, monitoring, and stepped interventions). Ethical and implementation challenges-privacy and consent, algorithmic bias and equity, governance, and the clinical consequences of false-positive and false-negative predictions-are discussed with an emphasis on safe deployment. We conclude with priorities for the field, including multimodal longitudinal cohorts, harmonized reporting standards, and pragmatic trials to determine whether AI decision support measurably improves suicide-prevention outcomes.

title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
desc: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
desc: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.

title: A Biologically Interpretable Single-Cell Pathology Foundation Model for Molecular Decoding of H&E Images
desc: The microscopic structure of human tissues encodes molecular information that is not directly accessible by visual inspection. Current pathology foundation models improve histological interpretation but operate at multicellular resolution. It remains unclear whether routine histology contains structured molecular and cellular information recoverable at single-cell resolution, which biological properties are associated with this recoverability, and where its limits lie. Here, we introduce Loki2, a single-cell pathology foundation model trained on UniSeg, a pan-tissue resource integrating 15 million cells with segmentation, lineage annotations and measured or histology-inferred transcriptomic profiles. We examine the above question across cellular representation, molecular recoverability, and patient-level relevance. Loki2 captures cellular identity and continuous morphological variation, with interpretable latent dimensions linked to physical nuclear phenotypes through DAPI validation. Transcriptomic retrieval and in silico protein staining test molecular recoverability, with gene-level analyses revealing the strongest recovery for genes associated with morphologically distinct cellular identities and functions. Then, patient staging and biomarker discovery connect cellular morphology representations to clinical relevance. Together, these findings establish Loki2 as a biologically interpretable single-cell pathology foundation model and provide the opportunities of recovering cellular and molecular information from routine H&E histology at single-cell resolution.

title: Eye-to-Eye: Gaze detection as a proxy for medical doctor behaviour during virtual and in-person appointments
desc: The gaze direction of the physician during consultations plays an important role in patient satisfaction, with several studies pointing to the positive correlation between the amount of time the physician spends looking at the patient and patient satisfaction. Additionally, the effects of the virtual consultation environment on the gaze behaviour of the doctor have yet to be studied. Therefore, this study aims to assess the impact of the virtual consultation environment by comparing the amount of total time the doctor spends looking at the patient between face-to-face and virtual consultations, as well as the average duration during the consultation and the gaze frequency. The study population consisted of 14 doctors divided between 4 medical specialties: Gynaecology/Obstetrics (4), Neurology (3), Endocrinology (3) and General and Familiar Medicine (4). A low-cost desktop that runs an appearance-based gaze estimation pipeline was implemented in the clinical setup. Each doctor recorded 20 face-to-face consultations and 20 virtual consultations, which were then processed by the pipeline to obtain the percentage of time the doctor spent looking at the patient during the consultation. Overall, we found that doctors look more at the patient in virtual consultations compared to face-to-face consultations, both in total time and average duration during the consultation. Within medical specialties, three out the four specialties involved presented clear tendencies to look more at the patient in virtual consultations when compared to face-to-face consultations.

Routine laboratory trajectories predict organ-level complications in cancer
desc: Routine laboratory panels drawn during cancer treatment constitute longitudinal physiological recordings of organ function, yet their temporal structure is discarded by single-timepoint prognostic tools. A transformer trained on 2,777,595 laboratory measurements from 3905 patients with multiple myeloma or ovarian cancer predicted which of 162 treatment-associated complications would be newly recorded within two years, spanning eight clinical categories, achieving 1.5- to 6.1-fold enrichment above prevalence. Across individual endpoints it exceeded non-sequential baselines, including engineered-trajectory models, by +0.024 to +0.070 in mean AUROC. Predictions generalised across both cancers, divergence concentrating in disease-specific complications, and biomarker masking recovered signatures consistent with established pathophysiology. External validation on MIMIC-IV and MMRF CoMMpass showed transferability, strongest for renal and metabolic endpoints, attenuated for infection endpoints. On CoMMpass it added prognostic value to ISS staging. Routine oncological laboratory data carry complication-specific physiological signal months before a complication is recorded, and require no testing beyond standard oncological care.

title: AI-guided CRISPR gene editing for cardiovascular disease: Current progress, transitional challenges, and future directions.
source: PubMed · American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice
desc: [American heart journal plus : cardiology research and practice] Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality despite major advances in pharmacological therapy, interventional cardiology, and lifestyle-based prevention. Although many current treatments reduce disease burden and improve outcomes, they often fail to address the underlying molecular and genetic mechanisms driving disease progression dot CRISPR hyphen-based gene- editing systems (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) have introduced the possibility of directly correcting, silencing, or modulating pathogenic genetic determinants involved in cardiovascular pathology. When integrated with artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled design, prediction, and optimization tools, an AI-guided CRISPR framework may assist in prioritizing editing strategies, predicting editing outcomes, and informing delivery design, although cardiovascular-specific validation of these applications remains limited. This narrative review examines the potential role of AI-guided CRISPR technologies in cardiovascular disease. It first outlines the major pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying CVD, then reviews molecular and genetic targets that may be amenable to editing. Current CRISPR applications in cardiometabolic and cardiovascular disorders are discussed, followed by an evaluation of how AI may support guide RNA design, off-target prediction, vector engineering, and therapeutic prioritization. Finally, major translational barriers are examined, including tissue-specific delivery, editing in non-dividing cells, long-term genomic safety, disease complexity, and regulatory implementation. Although early preclinical findings are encouraging, most cardiovascular applications remain in the experimental or early translational stage, and direct evidence for integrated AI-guided CRISPR applications in cardiovascular disease remains limited and largely preclinical. Progress in this field will depend on advances in delivery science, genome engineering, computational modelling, and long-term safety validation. AI-guided CRISPR should therefore be regarded as a developing precision medicine strategy with substantial future potential rather than an immediately deployable clinical solution.

title: When Expert Disagreement Hurts: Prestige and Selectivity in LLM Decision Revision
desc: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers. We introduce a controlled two-pass audit that holds the question, the evidence, and the model's initial answer fixed and varies only the revision context: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a domain expert. For binary decisions the accounting is exact: revision raises accuracy only if it is selective enough, reversing wrong answers more than a/(1-a) times as often as correct ones, where a is initial accuracy (nine times at 90%). Across five models and 1,989 evidence-grounded decisions in medicine, science, and law, no model clears this bar under expert disagreement, and accuracy falls by up to 16.1 points. The expert label, a prestige cue, adds reversals for four of the five models, yet its effect on accuracy ranges from a 5.2-point loss to a 2.4-point gain, so reversal counts are a poor proxy for harm. With identical arguments from both sources, the label still raises reversal for three proprietary models and in a pooled analysis of four newer models. Models also respond to stated source reliability. Revision pipelines should therefore be evaluated with paired, conditional metrics, per model and protocol.

title: PlainPairs: A Corpus Pairing the Prescriber and Patient Texts of U.S. Prescription Medicine Labels
desc: A prescription medicine in the United States comes with labeling written for prescribers, and many medicines also carry a text written for patients: a Medication Guide or a patient package insert. The two texts describe the same medicine for two readers, yet public resources rarely hold them side by side. I present PlainPairs, an open corpus built from the openFDA drug label files. Version 0.1.0 holds 35,177 prescription labels that carry a patient text, 21,416 distinct patient texts, 250,829 patient-text segments matched to prescriber sections through their regulatory headings, reading-level measures on both sides, and rule-based counts of plain-language wording. A second source, the National Cancer Institute's cancer information summaries, adds 756 summaries in health-professional and patient versions, in English and Spanish. Measured on the structure of the label, the median Medication Guide reads at grade 8.7 by Flesch-Kincaid and at grade 11.1 by SMOG. The same guides measured on the flattened text that the bulk files serve read about two grades higher, a difference that comes from lost list and heading boundaries. Patient texts address the reader in 41 of every 100 sentences, against 0.2 in prescriber sections. A blind hand check of 100 pairs supports the heading-based alignment for seven of ten heading types. The corpus, its code and its documents are public, and the release keeps texts that show a company copyright mark out of the text tables.

title: Savant: A Fast, Structure-Free Binding Affinity Predictor For Protein-Ligand Drug Screening
desc: Protein-ligand binding affinity determines which of many candidate molecules is worth synthesizing and assaying, making it the central measurement in early drug discovery. Binding affinity is commonly expressed as the dissociation constant, an equilibrium measure that indicates how easily a complex separates into its components. AI-based generative chemistry and make-on-demand chemical catalogs now produce molecules faster than rigorous method can evaluate them. Leading computational methods co-fold the complex before scoring the binding affinity between the protein and the ligand, which provides high accuracy but requires a graphics processing unit (GPU) and substantial time for every pair evaluated.Here we present Savant, a machine learning model that estimates the dissociation constant using only the protein's amino acid sequence and the ligand's structure written as a line of text (SMILES). Savant needs no 3-dimensional folded structure, no docking, and no GPU. To test Savant fairly, we built a benchmark designed to prevent any training data to leak into the testing set, drawing only on measurements published after the training data was assembled and on molecules chemically unlike anything the model had seen. On an independent benchmark, Savant ranks ahead of every other 3-dimensional structure-free method.Savant is designed to rank compounds against a single protein, and performs as well as other methods that require a GPU, while running only on a central processing unit (CPU). Thus, Savant can screen libraries of 100,000 compounds in minutes with commodity hardware.

title: Requirements of a knowledge support tool for self-harm in general practice: a mixed-methods study with patients, carers, and clinicians
desc: Background General practice has a central role in care following self-harm. However, clinicians frequently report uncertainty about best practice and patients describe poor care. A knowledge support tool is an add-on to electronic health systems that may improve services by providing personalised care information. Aim To understand what general practice clinicians, patients and carers need from a novel knowledge support tool for self-harm. Design and Setting Mixed-methods, using quantitative ratings, focus groups and follow-on interviews with general practice clinicians and patients/carers with lived experience of self-harm. Method Clinicians were recruited through social media and professional networks, and patients/carers through a third-sector organisation. During four focus groups and follow-on interviews, we explored the utility of potential content and functionality of a knowledge support tool. Quantitative utility ratings were summarised descriptively and qualitative data were analysed thematically using the framework method. People with lived/living experience were involved throughout. Results 13 clinicians and 14 patients/carers participated. Requirements of the knowledge support tool were captured across three qualitative themes: facilitating person-centred care, accessibility and usability, and balancing competing priorities of general practice. Across these themes, patients' and carers' needs were centred on promoting compassionate relationships and patient agency. Clinicians shared these needs but balanced them with a need to manage patient expectations and practice defensively under limited resources. Conclusion Our findings inform the core design of a knowledge support tool and suggest that such a tool could support the assessment and management of self-harm in general practice.

title: Artificial intelligence support for the prediction and management of drug-drug interactions.
source: PubMed · Expert opinion on drug metabolism & toxicology
desc: [Expert opinion on drug metabolism & toxicology] Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are a preventable cause of adverse drug events (ADEs), yet conventional interaction-checking tools are hampered by incomplete knowledge, poor concordance, and clinically unusable alert burdens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly utilized to strengthen multiple stages of the DDI pathway. This narrative review synthesizes literature identified through searches conducted between 15 July and 20 October 2026. It examines how machine learning (ML) predicts novel drug interactions from molecular structure and knowledge graphs; how natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs) identify and extract interactions from the literature, drug labels, and pharmacovigilance data; and how AI can make clinical decision support context-aware and support medication review. It also integrates mechanistic physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling and individualized patient-level risk prediction. Prediction models achieve impressive benchmark accuracy but frequently underperform in realistic, cold-start settings; LLMs detect interactions with high sensitivity but show poor severity calibration and persistent hallucination. The near-term value of AI lies less in autonomous prediction than in curating knowledge, personalizing alerts, and augmenting clinician judgment. Rigorous external validation, interpretability, and regulatory clarity are prerequisites for clinical adoption.

title: GlyphAtlas: Disentangling Stroke Detail from Layout for Scene Text Synthesis
desc: Scene text synthesis requires stroke-accurate characters rendered in a specified layout, as well as visual coherence with the surrounding scene. To achieve this, existing methods commonly pre-render the target text at its intended locations to form a glyph image that jointly specifies layout and glyph structure. However, this representation ties the resolution of each glyph to its target region, limiting fine-grained stroke guidance for small, densely packed, or structurally complex text. To tackle this, we propose GlyphAtlas, a scene text synthesis framework that retains the glyph image as a spatial anchor and supplies fine-grained stroke references through a dedicated glyph atlas. The atlas renders and encodes each character or word in a separate cell, decoupling reference resolution from target-region size. We further introduce atlas-anchored attention, which lets each text region retrieve stroke detail only from its corresponding atlas cells to refine the coarse glyph structure provided by the glyph image. This coarse-to-fine conditioning simplifies stroke rendering while preserving explicit layout correspondence. We optimize GlyphAtlas with a mask-weighted flow matching objective and a timestep-weighted text perceptual loss for writing accuracy and background consistency. Random resolution augmentation of atlas cells supports adjustable atlas budgets at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GlyphAtlas achieves stroke-accurate synthesis of small, dense, and structurally complex text, zero-shot transfer to languages unseen during task-specific training, and leading performance in scenes with many text regions. project page: https://fr0zencrane.github.io/project-glyphatlas/

title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
desc: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

title: Segment Anything for Microscopy 2
desc: Foundation models have advanced microscopy image segmentation, but existing models are trained on two-dimensional data, struggle with complex structures in volumetric data, and address only a narrow range of analysis tasks. Here we present Segment Anything for Microscopy 2 (SAM2), a foundation model that adapts SAM2 to joint 2D and 3D segmentation in light and electron microscopy. Trained on annotations of more than 23 million cells and nuclei and 1.6 million cellular structures, SAM2 achieves state-of-the-art automatic and interactive segmentation and outperforms generalist and specialist methods on volumetric data. Dedicated models further enable accurate mitochondrion and nucleus segmentation in electron microscopy. Beyond segmentation, SAM2 supports pixel and object classification from few annotations as well as cell tracking in 2D and 3D time-lapse data. All functionality is available in the user-friendly SAM napari plugin. We demonstrated the capabilities of SAM2 on challenging use cases spanning developmental biology, organoid research, cardiac physiology, and histopathology.

title: Microcirculation Mirror: A zero-install browser workstation for hand microvascular anatomy and nailfold capillaroscopy
desc: Background Hand microvasculature is conventionally presented through diagrams, cadaveric atlases and specialized optical instruments, while conventional clinical radiography cannot resolve individual capillary loops (5-15 m lumen) in vivo, which dominate cutaneous oxygen exchange. Methods We present Microcirculation Mirror, a zero-install browser workstation that registers layered hand anatomy to a live 21-landmark pose and couples it to a nailfold video capillaroscopy (NVC) simulator, a lumped microcirculatory model and an imaging-physics module. The single-file application runs offline on a laptop or, over local HTTPS, on a phone as an installable app. Results Its 3D atlas contains 136 named structures per hand in six systems from open Z-Anatomy/BodyParts3D meshes, plus a literature-parameterized capillary layer. The NVC module renders a 200x, 1.2-mm field with six deterministic patterns and quantified density, giant capillaries, avascular width fraction, hemorrhages, tortuosity and ramification. A lumped model reports nine estimates (SIM); a physics module shows that a 10-m capillary occupies 0.07 of a 150-m detector pixel; with iodinated contrast it retains {approx}0.016% effective contrast, about 60x below a 1% detection threshold; unenhanced blood is {approx}270x lower. The 2D stage renders in 2.9 ms per frame; system merging reduces atlas draw calls from 136 to 6. Conclusions The camera-overlay layers are templates, the atlas macro-anatomy is open mesh data, and the capillary layer is sampled. No patient data are used. The instrument is a product prototype, not a medical device, and provides a reproducible framework for making multi-scale microvascular reasoning visible.
