title: Exploring Artificial Intelligence Models for the Detection and Prediction of Sarcopenia: A Scoping Review.
desc: [Journal of clinical medicine] Background/Objectives: Sarcopenia is a progressive skeletal muscle disorder associated with adverse health outcomes, including disability, hospitalization, and mortality. Despite the availability of consensus-based diagnostic criteria, its identification in clinical practice remains limited due to reliance on specialized assessments and resource-intensive measurements. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) approaches have emerged as promising tools to enhance sarcopenia detection; however, evidence remains methodologically heterogeneous and has not been comprehensively synthesized. The objective was to systematically map the existing literature on AI/ML models developed to detect or predict sarcopenia, describing their methodological characteristics, input features, model performance, validation strategies, and adherence to reporting standards. Methods: A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Searches were performed in five databases (MEDLINE, Scopus, SciELO, Web of Science, and LILACS) from inception to 28 February 2026. Studies were included if they developed and/or validated AI/ML models for binary classification of sarcopenia using recognized consensus definitions. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed adherence to TRIPOD+AI reporting recommendations and appraised methodological quality using the NHLBI Quality Assessment Tool. Findings were synthesized descriptively. The review protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework. Results: Of 2910 records, 28 studies (n = 34,498 participants in the primary analytical cohorts, with an additional 2800 participants in independent external validation cohorts) were included, predominantly from Asia (China n = 14, South Korea n = 7). Random Forest was the most frequent algorithm (n = 6), followed by voting classifiers, MLP, and XGBoost (n = 4 each). Clinical tabular data, including anthropometric and laboratory variables, were the most common input features. Model performance was generally high, with AUC values ranging from 0.710 to 0.975 (mean ≈ 0.869), although heterogeneity across populations and validation strategies was substantial. External validation was performed in only 7 of the 28 studies (25%). No study fully adhered to TRIPOD+AI recommendations; mean compliance was moderate, with critical gaps in code sharing, patient/public involvement, external validation, and subgroup performance reporting. Conclusions: AI/ML models

title: Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in a Nigerian Cohort
desc: High-resolution brain MRI is important for neuroradiological assessment, yet routine clinical protocols often rely on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions, particularly in resource-constrained settings. These acquisitions may differ in orientation, alignment and anatomical coverage, resulting in partially overlapping image stacks. Existing learning-based super-resolution methods typically rely on single, under-constrained inputs or fixed multi-stack configurations with idealised acquisition geometry. We introduce MS-HVED, a sequence-agnostic framework for flexible multi-stack brain MRI super-resolution. Available axial, coronal and sagittal stacks are independently encoded into multi-scale Gaussian posteriors and fused using a field-of-view-aware Product-of-Gaussians formulation that limits contributions from unsupported regions. Physics-informed domain randomisation simulates heterogeneous clinical acquisition conditions, including obliqueness, partial coverage and imaging artefacts. MS-HVED achieved competitive or superior reconstruction fidelity across synthetic benchmarks and improved downstream tissue segmentation relative to low-resolution inputs. To assess generalisation beyond the training cohorts, we performed external clinical validation on 30 routine brain MRI examinations from a Nigerian cohort, representing an under-represented population in medical imaging research. These examinations formed the largest component of a blinded reader study involving 44 real cases and seven expert neuroradiologists. In the Nigerian cohort, MS-HVED was preferred over the supervised baseline for overall image quality in 187 of 210 paired assessments. Across all clinical cohorts, MS-HVED achieved higher overall-quality scores with all available inputs (5.93 vs. 4.49, p<.001), with the preference persisting when axial or coronal inputs were omitted (p<.001). Code at github.com/cai4cai/ms-hved

title: Sequence-based models predict TF binding with negligible contributions from motif cooperativity
desc: How transcription factors (TFs) selectively recognize their genomic targets among numerous sites containing similar DNA motifs remains an open question. Cooperative binding at neighboring motif sites is widely considered a key mechanism of TF specificity, yet its genome-wide contribution remains unclear. Machine learning models can now predict TF binding directly from DNA sequence, providing opportunities to investigate its underlying determinants. Here, we leveraged BPNet models trained on ~2,000 ENCODE TF binding profiles to systematically assess motif cooperativity. Although detected at individual loci, cooperativity made a negligible contribution to genome-wide binding predictions. Nevertheless, the models captured differences in binding preferences between TFs with similar motif preferences, even within the same cellular environment. These findings highlight the need to critically assess prevailing assumptions and explore alternative mechanisms underlying selective TF binding.

title: Uncertainty-aware longitudinal prediction of multiple adverse pregnancy outcomes
desc: Risk of pregnancy complications is reassessed at each antenatal visit, but whether earlier predictions add information beyond the most recent one is unclear. Classifying every prediction as low or high risk can leave uncertainty unexpressed. Whether reliability per visit holds across visits is also unclear. This secondary analysis included 9289 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort (eight US centres, 2010-2013). Logistic regression models predicted gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, suspected fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age at 6-13, 16-21 and 22-29 weeks (Visits 3). Mondrian conformal prediction reported 'no' (low risk), 'yes' (high risk), or both (review). To test whether prediction history adds information beyond the Visit 3 prediction, we compared, among women classified as high risk at Visit 3, those first classified as high risk at Visit 2 or 3 (emerging high) with those classified as high risk at all three visits (persistent high), adjusting for Visit 3 predicted probability. The adjusted proportion with the outcome was higher in the emerging-high than the persistent-high group, by 6.1 percentage points for large for gestational age (95% CI -0.4 to 12.2) and 3.8 percentage points for suspected fetal growth restriction (-0.9 to 8.1). Other outcomes showed adjusted differences close to zero. With conformal prediction calibrated to a 90% level at each visit, the reported answers included the actual outcome in 89.6-90.6% of women at each visit (coverage). Coverage decreased when each woman's three visits were considered together (79.0-85.4%). For fetal growth outcomes, how a woman's predicted risk evolved during pregnancy may add information beyond her Visit 3 prediction. For repeated clinical use, the target coverage level should reflect the acceptable risk of incorrect low- or high-risk classifications over a woman's follow-up and the clinical decisions supported at each visit.

title: STAT+: GOP, MAHA leaders clash over FDA nominee’s record on vapes
desc: White House health policy advisor facing uphill climb to become next FDA commissioner. Latest controversial issue is her work on flavored vapes.

title: FDA will move from AI to SI, but sponsors don’t have to follow
A Meta-Research Review of Statistical Practices for Image-Reliant AI Tools Predicting Lung Cancer Outcomes
desc: NEJM AI, Ahead of Print.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Cardiomyopathies: From Opportunistic Detection to Decision-Critical Risk Stratification.
desc: [Heart failure clinics] This article examines the evolving role of artificial intelligence (AI) across the continuum of care in cardiomyopathies, from opportunistic screening to decision-critical risk stratification. AI-enhanced electrocardiography enables scalable early detection, while advanced echocardiographic and cardiac magnetic resonance-based radiomics refine myocardial substrate characterization. Multimodal models integrating imaging, electrical, and clinical data refine risk stratification beyond conventional metrics such as left ventricular ejection fraction. However, clinical translation requires external validation, calibration stability, interpretability, and structured workflow integration. AI emerges not as autonomous diagnosis, but as accountable, clinician-supervised decision support embedded within multidisciplinary cardiovascular care.

title: FM-Recon: Exploring Foundation Model Features for Accelerated Cardiac Cine MRI Reconstruction
desc: Foundation models have demonstrated strong feature extraction capabilities across various medical imaging tasks, yet their potential for MRI reconstruction remains largely unexplored, particularly within unrolled reconstruction networks and under artifact-corrupted inputs. In this work, we explore whether and how features from pretrained foundation models can benefit accelerated cardiac cine MRI reconstruction. To this end, we propose FM-Recon, a framework that refines and integrates extracted features from frozen image encoder of foundation models into an unrolled reconstruction network. Through extensive experiments on the CMRxRecon2023 dataset, we systematically evaluate foundation model features across different reconstruction settings. Our results show that foundation models can extract informative representations from artifact-corrupted inputs and improve reconstruction performance, particularly at moderate acceleration factors. These findings demonstrate the potential of foundation model features for accelerated MRI reconstruction and provide insights into their effective integration into unrolled reconstruction networks.

title: Machine Learning Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance Genes: Performance, Interpretability, and Cross-Database Redundancy
desc: Antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) classifiers are typically developed and evaluated within a single curated database, leaving open how much two independently curated databases agree and what that implies for apparent cross-database generalization. We trained an XGBoost classifier on amino acid trigram frequencies and physicochemical descriptors using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), the field's largest curated ARG resource. The model separated resistance genes from non-resistance proteins with near-ceiling accuracy (AUROC = 0.982, MCC = 0.886); a label-shuffling null baseline collapsed to chance (AUROC = 0.508) and bootstrap confidence intervals were narrow, confirming genuine signal rather than data leakage or overfitting. SHAP analysis attributed this performance to biologically interpretable features, notably the trigram KTG, isoelectric point, and aromaticity, each consistent with known catalytic motifs in resistance enzymes. Before testing the classifier against ResFinder, one of CARD's most widely used counterparts, we assessed database independence by clustering sequences with CD-HIT, finding that 96.8-98.7% of ResFinder sequences shared substantial protein identity with CARD even at a permissive 50% identity threshold, indicating the two databases largely represent the same sequence population, with direct implications for how cross-database generalization should be measured. On the small subset of ResFinder sequences genuinely non-redundant with CARD (40-100 sequences, depending on threshold), the classifier failed completely, never classifying any as resistance genes; SHAP traced this failure to sequence length, as non-redundant sequences are nearly three times longer than training proteins, and length is among the model's most influential features. The same pattern emerged by resistance mechanism: the model achieved perfect accuracy on beta-lactamases, compact single-domain enzymes well represented in training (100%, n = 351), but correctly identified only 38.5% of efflux pump components (n = 13), a mechanism built from large, multi-domain transporters rather than compact catalytic enzymes. Together, these results describe a capable, interpretable ARG classifier alongside a quantified methodological caution: cross-database redundancy must be measured rather than assumed, and when a sequence-composition classifier fails, the failure is often explained by protein architecture rather than database origin.

title: FDA Launches Super Intelligence Hub, Details AI Governance and Internal Modernization Efforts
Comparative Cost of Care Recommended by Large Language Models versus Treating Physicians
desc: NEJM AI, Volume 3, Issue 11, November 2026.

title: Multiparametric 0.4-T low-field MRI mapping for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in rats.
desc: [European radiology experimental] Low-field MRI may broaden access to quantitative liver imaging, but low signal-to-noise ratio and coexisting steatosis, inflammation, fibrosis, and iron complicate relaxometry in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). We evaluated multiparametric 0.4-T MRI with deep-learning-reconstructed T1 mapping in rats. In this prospective cross-sectional preclinical study, 90 male Wistar rats underwent 0.4-T liver MRI during dietary induction, progression, and recovery. Metrics included native T1, fat-corrected T1 (FcT1), T2, T2*, and an apparent proton density fat fraction (PDFF) estimate. Whole-section digital pathology quantified steatosis, fibrosis, inflammation, and iron. Associations were assessed using iron-adjusted and stage-aware analyses, multivariable regression with variance inflation factors, and receiver operating characteristic analysis. Steatosis strongly correlated with T2 (ρ = 0.90, p 2.42% (0.77 versus 0.62; p = 0.008) and > 2.90% (0.78 versus 0.60; p = 0.001). Stage-aware analyses attenuated T1-fibrosis associations, and recovery animals showed residual fibrosis with near-baseline T1. Multiparametric 0.4-T MRI showed complementary, partly stage-dependent associations with MASLD pathology. T2/PDFF tracked steatosis; T2* retained an inflammation-related association after stage adjustment; and T1 elevation characterized active high-burden progression rather than isolated residual fibrosis. Human validation and platform calibration are required. Question Noninvasive MASLD assessment needs accessible imaging biomarkers that account for coexisting steatosis, inflammation, fibrosis, and iron-related confounding in liver MRI. Findings Multiparametric 0.4-T MRI showed complementary but stage-dependent associations: T2/apparent PDFF tracked steatosis, T2* related to inflammation, and T1 rose during high-burden progression. Relevance statement Multiparametric 0.4-T MRI provides complementary pathology-correlated measurements for MASLD assessment in rats, but reconstruction-dependent T1 bias and apparent PDFF estimation require platform calibration and human validation before clinical interpretation.

title: A Crowd-Audited Atlas of Implicit Bias in LLM-Powered Agents
desc: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.

title: Pharmacophore-Inspired Virtual Receptor: Generating Realistic Peptide Binding Data for Machine Learning
desc: VReceptor is a virtual receptor simulation framework that generates realistic, sequence-dependent binding data for peptide-based therapeutics. It combines pharmacophore-inspired weighting schemes with amino acid similarity metrics to evaluate peptide design strategies in a controlled environment. Validation using the Prolactin-Releasing Peptide (PrRP) dataset confirms VReceptor's ability to approximate binding behaviours and optimize experimental planning. This framework empowers researchers in computational peptide design and active learning workflows while highlighting areas for further refinement.

title: Cardio Diagnostics to Unveil Non-Obstructive Coronary Artery Disease Data, FDA Breakthrough Device Designation Strategy, and India Launch Update on December 10 Investor Call
The Formal-Functional Gap: How Artificial Intelligence Reshapes Medical Professional Identity.
source: PubMed · Advances in medical education and practice
desc: [Advances in medical education and practice] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into clinical practice and medical education, yet research on AI and medical professional identity has largely evolved in parallel. To examine how AI is transforming fundamental components of medical professional identity and propose a framework for understanding its implications for professional identity formation in medical education. This narrative review synthesizes conceptual, empirical, and theoretical literature on AI, professional identity formation, and clinical practice through iterative literature searching and citation tracking. Peer-reviewed studies, regulatory data, and national survey reports were considered. AI affects professional identity unevenly. Diagnostic, predictive, generative, and emerging autonomous systems most directly influence expertise, clinical reasoning, and professional autonomy, shifting physicians from exclusive holders of specialized knowledge toward validators of increasingly accessible but variably trusted information. Evidence of automation bias and reduced diagnostic performance highlights this transition. We conceptualize the divergence between the formal locus of clinical responsibility, which remains with physicians, and the functional locus of influence decisions, shared with AI, as the formal-functional gap (FFG). Its magnitude varies by AI configuration, identity component, and career stage, potentially placing trainees at risk of never-skilling and experienced physicians at risk of deskilling. Ethical responsibility, humanistic care, lifelong learning, and professional authority are affected more indirectly. AI-mediated professional identity change reflects a dynamic interaction between physicians' developmental trajectories and evolving AI capabilities. Medical education should prioritize sustained expertise, clinical reasoning, professional autonomy, AI-interpretive judgment, and human oversight. The FFG remains a conceptual framework whose relationships require empirical validation.

title: A Generative AI-Driven Architecture for Whole-Home Intelligent Services: Edge Models, Memory Management, and Household Applications
desc: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.

title: Casanovo-TMT: deep learning-based de novo sequencing of TMTpro-labeled peptides and phosphopeptides
desc: De novo peptide sequencing reads peptides directly from tandem mass spectra, but none of the released deep learning models can sequence peptides labeled with isobaric tags such as TMTpro, which are widely used for multiplexed quantitative proteomics. We extended the residue vocabulary of Casanovo with TMTpro tags and phosphorylation, fine-tuned it on 21 million spectra from our laboratory, most of them TMTpro-labeled, and re-ranked the candidates in the beam by their agreement with the measured precursor mass. The resulting model, Casanovo-TMT, predicted the exact peptidoform for 84.7% of the TMTpro-labeled spectra in our test set and for 87.4 and 79.6% of the spectra in two public global-proteome datasets from other laboratories, whereas the extended vocabulary without fine-tuning gave 0.3%. Discarding the lowest-scoring predictions raised precision to 95% while retaining 81.7% of the test spectra. Casanovo-TMT also predicted the exact peptidoform for 69.2% of the spectra in a public phosphopeptide-enriched dataset and for 66 to 72% of the phosphopeptide spectra in three phosphoproteomic studies from our laboratory that were not used for training. In these studies, it identified numbers of phosphopeptides comparable to or larger than those of database search engines, and proportionally more where database search identified fewer. For the phosphopeptides identified only by Casanovo-TMT, entrapment estimated that more than 90% were correct, and an independent search engine assigned the same sequence to 95 to 98% of the spectra that it identified with confidence. Casanovo-TMT can therefore extend database search in TMTpro-based quantitative proteomics, particularly in studies in which database search identifies few phosphopeptides.

title: FDA to refer to AI as ‘super intelligence’ going forward
Hydrogel-based biosensors for sweat analysis in sports medicine: recent advances and future prospects.
desc: [Designed monomers and polymers] Sweat is a physiological fluid that can be collected non-invasively and is continuously secreted by the human body. It contains a wide variety of biomarkers, including electrolytes, metabolites, hormones, and proteins, which may provide complementary information about physical activity and selected aspects of physiological status. In recent years, wearable biosensors based on hydrogels have drawn increasing interest in exercise monitoring and sports medicine because of the material's flexibility, hydrophilicity, and biocompatibility. This review summarizes recent advances in hydrogel-based sweat detection, highlighting sensing mechanisms and representative applications for four major biomarker categories: electrolytes, metabolites, hormones, and proteins. It also discusses potential applications in hydration assessment, fatigue-related monitoring, sports-injury risk assessment, and rehabilitation management. The discussion addresses current challenges, including material durability, signal stability, physiological interpretation, clinical translation, and large-scale manufacturing. Looking ahead, future progress will likely focus on multifunctional hydrogels, integration with artificial intelligence and data-driven methods, personalized monitoring, and standardized testing and validation protocols. Overall, hydrogel-based sweat biosensing offers a promising complementary approach for non-invasive physiological monitoring, although broader sports-medicine use will require rigorous validation under real-world exercise conditions.

title: Towards wearable-scale, transition-aware sleep staging for clinical populations
desc: Automatic sleep staging models are predominantly developed on healthy sleepers and generalize poorly to clinical populations with fragmented sleep. Across three cohorts (patients with stroke, isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder, and other sleep disorders), we observe 2-3x more awakenings per hour, nearly twice as much N1, and less REM sleep than in healthy sleepers. We propose a label-efficient teacher-student framework for wearable-scale sleep staging. SleepGPT (136M parameters), adapted using labels from 25% of training patients, supervises a causal CNN-GRU (31k parameters; 122 KB) that stages EEG, EOG, or both in real time. We introduce Gcv-TAD, a new black-box transition-aware distillation loss. It emphasizes uncommon stage transitions while discounting those that vary across patients, using a prior estimated from labelled patients. In patient-wise 10-fold cross-validation, Gcv-TAD improves per-patient macro F1 over supervised training on the same labels by +3.2 to +7.6 points on average. Gains are largest on N1, and performance approaches full-label training.

title: Medtronic announces FDA clearance of general surgery procedures for the Hugo robotic-assisted surgery system
Breaking the rules by design: the evolution of Lipinski's principles toward modern drug discovery.
source: PubMed · Expert opinion on drug discovery
desc: [Expert opinion on drug discovery] Lipinski's Rule of Five (Ro5) has long framed the characteristics of orally administered drugs; however, many clinically relevant targets, particularly protein-protein interactions and other complex interfaces, require compounds operating in chemical space beyond this rule. Understanding how these drugs surpass classical thresholds while maintaining efficacy and pharmacokinetics is a fundamental aspect of modern drug discovery. This narrative review is based on a literature using PubMed/Medline between 2016 and 2026. The DrugBank database was also used as an illustrative, retrospective case study to examine how literature-derived bRo5 principles are reflected in approved drugs. The review focuses on five key modalities: optimized small molecules, natural products, peptides/peptidomimetics, macrocycles, and proteolysis-targeting chimeras. Approved bRo5 drugs illustrate that the classic Ro5 should be reconsidered as a context-dependent guideline rather than a universal filter. In the authors' view, future discovery campaigns targeting complex biological targets should move away from rigid thresholds and adopt a deliberate bRo5 design, prioritizing control of hydrogen bonds, 3D shape, and chameleonicity over simple compliance scores. Integrating high-quality structural data with Artificial Intelligence-driven physics-based models may be particularly valuable for rationally expanding the bRo5 chemical space, reducing reliance on empirical trial-and-error, and addressing inaccessible targets to conventional small molecules.

title: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls
desc: Autonomous voice agents now conduct routine clinical follow-up calls, so some automated triage is unavoidable. A patient becoming frustrated is one thing that triage should catch. These systems typically read only the transcript the speech-to-text stage produces, not the voice, and whether that is enough is largely untested on real clinical speech. We study per-turn frustration detection on real patient calls from a deployed clinical voice agent: 150 turns from six calls labelled by three annotators, with a length-matched acted corpus as a control, and 714 turns from 30 calls. Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

title: Smartphone-Only Essential Tremor Tracking Secures FDA 510(K) Clearance
Machine learning-guided discovery of TMX4@G electrocatalysts with LLM-assisted workflow automation.
desc: [Nanoscale] Coordination-engineered transition-metal single-atom catalysts offer a modular platform for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), but their discovery is hindered by the large configurational space arising from coupled metal-ligand variations. Here we develop a symmetry-aware and uncertainty-guided workflow to accelerate the screening of TMX4@G catalysts (X = C, N, O, P or S), where a transition-metal atom is coordinated by four ligands embedded in graphene. Canonicalization of rotationally equivalent motifs reduces 17 500 nominal structures to 4900 symmetry-inequivalent candidates while preserving chemical diversity. A cascaded Gaussian process regression model encodes a physical hierarchy from atomic descriptors to electronic structure, metal-hydrogen interaction and the HER activity. Posterior uncertainty drives active learning by balancing near-thermoneutral hydrogen binding with exploration of underrepresented coordination motifs. A large language model (LLM)-assisted automation framework further integrates structure generation, VASP input preparation, job submission, output parsing and dataset updating. DFT validation shows strong agreement with model predictions (R2 = 0.898 for 24 candidates) and identifies six thermodynamically stable catalysts with ηHER < 0.15 V.

title: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
desc: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.

title: Comments on FDA’s PMA eSTAR Draft Guidance
Gender and Valuation in Venture Capital.
source: PubMed · The British journal of sociology
desc: [The British journal of sociology] Recent work in the sociology of finance draws attention to the speculative valuations associated with venture capital (VC) investments. Yet the fact that the VC ecosystem is dominated by men is persistently overlooked. This paper redresses the largely gender-blind sociology of valuation in financing by focusing on investors and startups in the much-hyped market of Artificial Intelligence. Our aim is to show how gender matters in performative market-making. Drawing on in-depth interviews with men and women involved in high-tech financing, we analyse the structural impediments to successful female pitching, valuation, and work in VC. By zooming in on the microprocesses of financialization, valuation and assessment, we shed new light on how the mechanisms involved in the assessment of high-tech startups impact female founders. Our study finds that women are excluded through shifting reference to one of several social mechanisms in a practice we call 'rationale roulette': reliance upon future-oriented narratives that can only be persuasively performed by men, embeddedness within homogenous male-dominated networks, and relegation of feminized pathways to the sidelines. In the highly uncertain world of VC investments, valuations based on gender ultimately transmute into a hedge against risk. We conclude with implications for economic sociologies of finance, the innovation sector, and sociotechnical systems, as scholars must recognize the constitutive status of gender and other social characteristics to better understand local valuation mechanisms and their implications for the sector.

title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
desc: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

title: Generating machine-learning-ready enzyme sequence-function data from microdroplet screening.
desc: [Methods in enzymology] If enzyme engineering is to achieve the goal of making enzyme reactivity truly 'programmable', large, quantitative sequence-function datasets will be indispensable to train and validate predictive models. Droplet microfluidics can measure millions of genotype-bearing compartments, but quantitative sequence-function data with an accurate error estimate requires coordination between library construction, sorting, sequencing and analysis. This chapter describes a practical workflow for connecting full-length enzyme sequences to droplet phenotypes and converting the resulting barcode-assigned read counts into quantitative fitness estimates with defined uncertainty - turning droplet microfluidics into a data generation device. The approach is not restricted to conventional deep mutational scanning: beyond single mutations, libraries may contain combinatorially mutagenised variants of a parent enzyme, fully synthetic genes or sequences recovered from metagenomic libraries. A previous long-read deep mutational scanning (lrDMS) campaign followed by machine-learning that was used to generate combinatorial sequence-function data is used to illustrate a practical implementation of data harvesting from a library screening experiment. We give recommendations for experimental planning and execution covering oversampling, gating, library skew, library cloning and barcode design and emphasise experimental and computational quality controls that identify noise or bias in the dataset that would jeopardise interpretability when they propagate into a machine-learning dataset.

title: Fix, Don't Retake: Physics-Simulated Training for Correcting Patient Positioning Errors in Dental Panoramic Radiographs
desc: Patient-positioning errors can distort panoramic radiographs and lead to repeat examinations. This study investigated artificial intelligence for correcting these errors in existing images. A physics-based simulator generated paired correctly positioned and mispositioned panoramics from cone-beam computed tomography volumes, with controlled individual and combined positioning errors. Five approaches were compared: U-Net, pix2pix, conditional diffusion, an error-conditioned model, and a mixture of error-specific specialists. Evaluation used image similarity and geometric metrics across three test sets. All approaches improved mean image similarity and reduced geometric errors, with U-Net and the two error-aware approaches outperforming pix2pix and conditional diffusion.

title: Validating LLM-Based Essay Scorers: A Comparative Analysis in Critical Online Reasoning in Medical Education
desc: Automated essay scorers (AES) based on large language models (LLMs) promise human-level accuracy. However, training, fine-tuning, and evaluating LLMs for specific assessment tasks is costly. In particular, the question arises whether these AES should be trained for specific domains or whether models based on generic LLMs might be sufficient. Human annotations, by contrast, are often more valid but far more expensive. This study evaluates whether ensembles of AES systems based on general-purpose LLMs can approximate human ratings of medical-education writing tasks by leveraging encoded linguistic and conceptual knowledge. The goal is to assess whether general-purpose models are applicable for assisting or potentially replacing human annotation in this domain. We experiment with 11 AES systems and 8 different LLMs and evaluate 668 student responses to 12 tasks, using \numprint{2076} evaluations by 7 human annotators. These ratings are aggregated to create consistent performance levels that can be used as target classes for classifiers trained on AES outputs. Our results show that learner classes based on human ratings can be accurately reconstructed using a linear SVM trained on a small set of AES features. A single classifier generalized well across tasks and domains, with reasoning and content features being most predictive. This suggests that out-of-the-box LLMs, even without domain-specific fine-tuning, can support automatic essay grading in medical education. While individual AES systems are insufficient alone, their combination approximates human evaluators, pointing to a reduced need for manual scoring or its supplementation with automated methods.

title: Scribble Once, Segment the Sequence: Bidirectional Temporal Consistency for Weakly Supervised Segmentation in Echocardiography Sequences
desc: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.

title: FH-Sampling: Frequency-aware Hypergraph-driven Oversampling for Imbalanced Time-Series Classification
desc: Imbalanced time-series data appears commonly in diverse applications, such as medical diagnosis. When trained on imbalanced data, classifiers tend to exhibit a bias toward the majority class, making it difficult to identify minority-class instances accurately, despite their critical importance. Sampling techniques have proven effective in rebalancing imbalanced data. However, existing interpolation-based oversampling methods typically rely on pairwise interpolation, limiting their ability to capture high-order inter-sample relationships, and their inherent smoothing effects tend to suppress high-frequency components, compromising spectral fidelity. Therefore, we propose a Frequency-aware Hypergraph-driven Oversampling method (FH-Sampling) for imbalanced time-series classification. In FH-Sampling, a hypergraph is first constructed in the original time-series space to capture complex high-order inter-sample relationships, and sampling ratios are adaptively assigned to mitigate the impact of noisy samples. The discrete wavelet transform decomposes each sample into frequency components. Guided by the sample hypergraph, FH-Sampling combines high-frequency components from related samples while retaining the target sample's low-frequency component to help preserve important frequency characteristics. Experiments on 24 imbalanced datasets demonstrate the advantages of FH-Sampling for imbalanced time-series classification. We further apply FH-Sampling to aircraft trajectory generation. Experiments on simulated aircraft trajectories show that FH-Sampling produces trajectories that better match the real distribution, highlighting its potential for practical applications.

title: When Do Histology Foundation Models Need Geometric Test-Time Augmentation?
desc: Test-time augmentation (TTA) aggregates model predictions across multiple transformed views of an input during inference. Because histology images lack a canonical orientation, $D_4$ TTA---pooling across the 8 rotations and reflections of a square---is a standard default in computational pathology. However, the rise of self-supervised histology foundation models (FMs) with inherent rotational invariance calls its continued utility into question. We benchmark 9 histology FMs and 6 general-purpose models across four patch-level and two whole-slide image (WSI) datasets. We find that $D_4$ TTA remains a reliable post hoc improvement, but benefits diminish from $+1.98$ percentage points (pp) for general-purpose backbones to $+0.50$ pp for histology FMs on TCGA-UT, and shrink further for the largest models. To eliminate computational overhead, our experiments demonstrate that entropy routing---applying TTA selectively to uncertain predictions---recovers most of the gain while augmenting only ${\sim}13\%$ of samples. Finally, we show that patch-level TTA improvements do not transfer to slide-level multiple instance learning (MIL). Code: https://github.com/lars-chen/histology-tta

title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks
desc: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.

title: What You Post Is What You Symptom: Estimating Psychometric Networks from Social Media Discourse
desc: Symptom networks in psychopathology are estimated almost exclusively from self-report questionnaires, restricting inference to whatever symptom set a given instrument covers. We introduce a framework for symptom-resolved network estimation directly from social media discourse and apply the framework to depression and eating disorders, with a third anorexia corpus as cross-dataset validation. To our knowledge, we are the first to estimate symptom-resolved psychometric networks from social media text, compare them to clinical co-endorsement networks, and replicate transdiagnostic linguistic markers across 3 independently recruited corpora spanning 2 disorders simultaneously. For depression, expression scores correlate with BDI-II totals at $ρ{=}0.434$, 20 of 21 items reach FDR significance, and split-half reliability is 0.935. The Network Comparison Test detects few edge differences between modalities (3-5\% of edges), while bridge symptoms diverge. For eating disorders, the item-level results are exploratory. Identified linguistic features replicate the same direction across all 3 corpora, and they cluster in three construct families.

title: State-Message Interaction Adapter for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation
desc: Cross-domain few-shot segmentation adapts natural-image pretrained encoders to medical or industrial domains from a few pixel-annotated support masks. Within frozen DINOv3, intermediate per-head attention messages already carry target-background distinctions that baseline final-layer similarities and predictions do not consistently reflect. We propose the State-Message Interaction Adapter (SMIA) to learn how per-head messages should update each receiving token representation while keeping pretrained attention and FFN parameters frozen. Inserted right after per-head aggregation, SMIA conditions the transformation of each head's aggregated output (message) on each patch's pre-attention feature (state), allowing similar contextual messages to produce distinct or opposing updates depending on the receiving position. Because scarce support masks cover only limited state-message combinations, a shared low-rank bilinear map confines the learned interactions to low-dimensional state, message, and output subspaces. Added before each adapted block's frozen FFN, these updates yield adapted features that are refined by frozen FFNs and deeper blocks for linear readout. With only 0.51M trainable parameters and single-pass, support-free inference, SMIA achieves six-dataset mean mIoUs of 77.40% at 5 shots and 80.99% at 10 shots across 20 medical and industrial tasks, surpassing the strongest prior methods by +3.61 and +3.93 percentage points. In controlled 10-shot comparisons across three benchmarks on the same DINOv3 backbone, SMIA also outperforms parameter-matched AdaptFormer, LoRA, and ParaX with a better precision-recall balance.

title: MedJev: A System One Vision-Language Decision Model for Fast and Effective Medical Image Understanding
desc: Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce \textsc{MedJev}, a \emph{system one} vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, \textsc{MedJev} removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, \textsc{MedJev}-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of \textbf{7.93\%} and a \textbf{6.04$\times$} end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that \textsc{MedJev}-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.

title: Medical question answering collapses in Hausa: a pre-registered pilot on three small open models
desc: A system that reads nothing and always answers the most frequent letter scores \BaselineP{} on our Hausa medical multiple-choice set. \NBelowBaseline{} of the \NModels{} small open models we evaluate do not beat it. We lead with that because the usual summary of a multilingual result -- a percentage-point drop from English -- does not say whether what survives the drop is performance at all. On a paired English--Hausa set of \NEval{} MedMCQA items, three instruction-tuned models of 3--4B parameters lose between \GapMedGemma{} and \GapQwen{} points of accuracy, every gap significant after Holm correction. Back-translating the Hausa items into English recovers between half and two-thirds of the gap for the two general-purpose models but not demonstrably for the medically adapted one, so the deficit is substantially, though not wholly, a matter of the language of presentation. Answers are also far less stable: agreement across three option orderings falls from \ConsEnQwen{} to \ConsHaQwen{} in the worst case. An exploratory error analysis of \ENRows{} discordant items attributes most of the damage to medical vocabulary lost in translation (\ETerm{}, 95\% CI \ETermLo{}--\ETermHi{}), usually in the question stem. A fourth registered hypothesis proposed closing the gap with self-generated preference pairs. Its pilot gate found nothing to train on: asked to reason in Hausa rather than to pick a letter, the model echoes the prompt back, switches into Swahili, or simply stops without answering; only \GateParse{} of chains are parseable. We report that intervention as not run, which is itself the sharper result -- a forced-choice benchmark cannot see a model that has no generative command of the language at all. All hypotheses, thresholds and decision rules were registered before any model was run, and all deviations are logged.

title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
desc: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.
